Many people believe that if you work hard, make good choices, and contribute to your community, you ought to be rewarded for your efforts. The problem is that we don't start life on an even playing field. Imagine competing in a race, except some people get the good fortune of getting to start just a few feet from the finish line, while you're stuck several hundred meters back.

There are several reasons why one might be put at a relative advantage or disadvantage, but one of the primary contributors is capital. If you are lucky enough to be born into a wealthy family with connections, you are very likely to live a comfortable, safe, happy life because of the stability, support and opportunities afforded to you; on the other hand, if you have the misfortune to be born into poverty to a single mother working two minimum wage jobs to make ends meet, your prospects are much bleaker. You have virtually no support system, you never know when you'll be evicted, you might not know where your next meal is coming from (assuming you get one at all). Suddenly, the resident drug dealers are your heroes. They can afford rent. They can afford food. They're popular. The have everything they want. Meanwhile, the police and authority become your worst enemy. They take away your friends, terrorize your neighbors, and make life that much more hellish.

In poverty, the role of institutions change from the functions they serve in polite society. Going to prison is seen as a badge of honor, a way to augment one's street cred. However, going to prison does provide shelter, and means that there's one less mouth for the family to feed. Meanwhile, the school systems around those in poverty are falling apart. Generally, they are funded by property taxes. It turns out poor people don't have a lot of money to spend on property, and so schools fall into disrepair, and the education they receive is merely the twisted shadow of that received within the walls of an elite private school. And forget about getting a good job. At that level, there is no such thing as job security, no benefits to speak of, and the gross disregard of labor laws runs rampant. With poor education comes a poor job, which leads to the cycle of poverty being perpetuated. There is no more reason to have faith in an employer as there is to have faith in the police. For these people the entire system is broken.

So what's to be done about this? How do we make sure that everyone gets to start the race on even terms? Many say that socialism (or at least parts of it) could significantly contribute to assuaging the inequality inherent both in America and the world over. To recall socialism is an economic system in which government own the means of production. That is to say, there is still private property, but the government owns the business and non-profit functions of society. Now, that's full socialism. The truth is that almost no one is for that. In fact there are already a select few industries in the US that are socialized (and there is no country in the world for which this is not the case). What Sanders is talking about is an expansion of this, for example, making prisons a public enterprise only. The abuse that people face behind bars and the draconian policies that are pushed by corporate lobbyists in the name of profits which drive incarceration rates are too much to allow this function to be privatized. Sanders and his supporters believe it is better that government handle these sorts of affairs rather than the free market because of the latter's ability to use monitor and regulate operations (as well as the philosophical underpinnings of our justice system).

There's much more at work here than what I just described, but this should provide a reasonable baseline for understanding why some people think socialist policies are a good idea. You don't have to agree with it, but we (for I include myself among them) believe we have some valid points. Remember, we are all Americans. We may disagree, but we only argue so passionately because we all want what's best for our country. We just occasionally disagree as to exactly what that happens to be.
People want equality of outcome not equality of a playing field and life just doesn't work that way.
